title: Why Tomato Seeds Sometimes Sprout Inside the Tomato

seo.title: Why Tomato Seeds Sprout Inside the Fruit
seo.meta_description: Seeds can germinate inside an overripe tomato when dormancy weakens and moisture, warmth, and hormones favor growth. The phenomenon is called vivipary.
seo.search_intent: Understand why tomato seeds sometimes germinate inside the fruit and whether the tomato is still usable.

excerpt: Tiny green or white sprouts inside a tomato are a case of vivipary: the seeds began germinating before leaving the fruit. It is a physiological oddity favored by advanced ripeness and suitable temperature and moisture.
content_html:
Tomato seeds can occasionally germinate while they are still inside the fruit, producing tiny roots or shoots before the tomato is cut open. Botanists call this precocious germination or vivipary. It happens when the normal mechanisms that keep a mature seed dormant are no longer strong enough to prevent growth.

The tomato supplies moisture and the seed already contains an embryo and stored reserves. If ripeness, temperature, and hormonal balance line up, germination can begin inside what is effectively a moist enclosed chamber.

Seeds normally remain dormant because the fruit suppresses germination

A mature tomato seed is capable of becoming a new plant, but it usually does not start growing inside a healthy fruit. Seed coats, chemical inhibitors, plant hormones, and the surrounding fruit environment help delay germination until the seed is dispersed.

Abscisic acid is one of the hormones strongly associated with maintaining seed dormancy, while gibberellins promote germination and growth. As fruit ages and seed physiology changes, the balance can shift. Genetic differences between varieties can also make precocious germination more or less likely.

Once inhibition weakens, the seed already has access to water. Warm conditions can then make the interior suitable for the first stages of growth even though the seed has not reached soil.

Overripeness and storage conditions make vivipary more likely

Vivipary is often noticed in tomatoes that have remained ripe for a long time. As the fruit advances beyond ideal eating quality, tissues soften and the chemical environment around the seeds changes. Long warm storage can provide additional time for germination to begin.

The first sign may be a white root emerging from a seed. If growth continues, pale or green shoots can curl through the seed cavities. These structures can look worm-like at first glance, but they are plant seedlings attached to the tomato's own seeds.

The phenomenon is not unique to tomatoes. Precocious germination occurs in peppers, squash, citrus, and other fruits under certain conditions, although the triggers vary among species.

A sprouted tomato is not automatically rotten, but quality still matters

The sprouts themselves are evidence of seed germination, not proof of microbial spoilage. A tomato can show vivipary while the flesh remains free of mold or foul odor. However, the condition often appears in fruit that is very ripe, so texture and flavor may already be past their best.

Inspect the whole tomato. If it smells normal and has no mold, slime, leaking decay, or sour fermentation, the germination is mainly a quality issue. Many people simply discard the sprouts and use sound flesh in cooked dishes.

If the fruit is badly softened, moldy, leaking, or unpleasant-smelling, discard it because those are separate deterioration signs. Germinated seeds do not make other spoilage indicators irrelevant.

The seedlings can sometimes continue growing outside the fruit

If the germinated seeds are healthy enough, they may continue growing when removed and placed in a suitable growing medium. Whether they produce plants true to the parent depends on the tomato variety and whether it was a hybrid.

For eating purposes, there is no need to rescue or cultivate them. Vivipary simply reveals that a mature seed's developmental clock has started before dispersal rather than afterward.

The surprising sprouts are therefore a timing problem, not a mysterious infestation. The seed became physiologically ready to grow while still surrounded by the tomato. Judge the fruit's usability by normal spoilage signs rather than by germination alone.

faq.question: Are the little sprouts inside a tomato worms?
faq.answer: No. When they are attached to tomato seeds, they are usually roots or shoots from seeds that have germinated inside the fruit.

faq.question: Can you eat a tomato with sprouted seeds?
faq.answer: The sprouts alone do not prove spoilage. If the surrounding flesh is normal and free from mold or bad odor, the issue is mainly quality, although very ripe fruit may taste poorer.

faq.question: What is vivipary in tomatoes?
faq.answer: It is precocious seed germination that begins before the seed has left the fruit.
